analysis.title: 2027 Global Economics Outlook: Powered by AI, Tested by Oil
key_insights: Baseline: global growth stays solid (global real GDP 3.5% in 2026E, 3.4% in 2027E and 2028E), with US strength insulating the rest of the world. Developed-market central banks begin a modest hiking cycle because inflation is persistently high after the energy shock.
The view of a brief tightening cycle depends on energy prices continuing to fall. Inflation risks are skewed to the upside, and the risk that inflation crimps growth is rising.

US growth is driven by AI-related capex and consumption by high-income households supported by wealth and full employment. MS expects US real GDP of 2.5% 4Q/4Q in 2027 versus 2.6% in 2026, then 2.7% in 2028.

Developed-market policy rates are forecast to peak in 1Q27: Fed 4.25-4.5% (4.375% midpoint), ECB deposit rate 3.0%, BoJ 1.75%. Most economies are then projected to begin a modest cutting cycle in 2028.
Fed baseline: 25bp hikes in December 2026 and March 2027, then a hold through 2027. First cut in 2Q28, taking the rate to 3.625% by end-2028 (3.50-3.75% range).

ECB baseline: 25bp hikes in December 2026 and March 2027 to 3.0%, a hold until June 2028, then quarterly cuts to 2.25% by 4Q28. Euro area headline inflation peaks above 4% in early 2027 and core stays above target until mid-2028.

BoE baseline: hikes in December 2026 and February 2027 to 4.50%, a hold through 2027, and easing from 2Q28. BoJ baseline: 25bp hikes in December 2026 and March 2027 to 1.75%, then a pause. Japan headline inflation falls below 2% from 2H27.

Oil on the screen is no longer a sufficient statistic. Refining spreads are historically wide and diesel is expected to stay tight into mid-2027, so crude falling may not lower fuel costs quickly. This is why central banks find it hard to look through the oil shock.

Producer prices are rising in energy-exposed sectors (chemicals, rubber, plastics, transport). Buffers from inventories, hedges, fixed-price contracts and fiscal support have been used up. Pass-through into core inflation has not yet broadly appeared, but the US shows early signs in core goods. Europe is most exposed and Asia least.

AI investment: hyperscaler capex forecast at $1.6tn in 2027 and $1.8tn in 2028, with annual growth slowing sharply from 2027 to 2028. MS shifted 5GW of US data center projects from 2028 to 2029, leaving US data center capex flat 2027 to 2028 and up about 40% in 2029. This is a delay, not a pause.

In 3Q26 AI investment contributed 1.6pp to US growth before imports and 0.9pp after. The GDP contribution of AI peaks around 2027, then rotates from infrastructure toward software and adoption from 2028.

AI-linked goods are nearly one quarter of US imports and have driven all import growth since 2025. Mexico supplies roughly half of US server imports. Taiwan and Korea are the main beneficiaries, with Japan and Europe gaining exposure in equipment and power infrastructure.

US productivity: trend growth is about 2.1% (1.6% in 2019), with the baseline assuming 2.3% by 2028. Industries with high AI exposure contributed 2.0pp of the 2.4% rise in output per employee over the four quarters to 2Q26. The gains are mainly capital deepening, and the broad total factor productivity pickup has not yet emerged.

AI labor displacement is micro rather than macro: MS estimates AI has raised the aggregate unemployment rate by no more than 15bp through 1H26, concentrated among younger workers. The US labor market is 'slow-hire/slow-fire' with payroll breakeven near 50k a month and unemployment of 4.3% in 2027 and 4.4% in 2028.

US consumption: wealth effects added about 0.6pp to real consumption growth over the four quarters to 3Q26 (household net worth about $195tn). Real consumption growth slows from 2.4% in 2026 to 2.0% in 2027, with low- and middle-income households driving the slowdown.

US core PCE is forecast to fall from 3.2% at end-2026 to 2.6% at end-2027 (2.2% at end-2028). Residual seasonality is expected to make 1Q27 inflation readings opaque. Headline CPI 4Q/4Q is 3.9% in 2026, 2.1% in 2027.

MS's estimate of the US real neutral rate has risen to about 1.5% (about 3.5% nominal), so current policy is neutral to modestly restrictive. A sustained productivity acceleration would raise r*, and the case for a higher neutral rate is stronger than confidence in its level.

Scenario 1, Aggregate Demand upside: US unemployment falls to 3.5%, core inflation stays just above 3%, and the Fed hikes to 5.625% by end-2027 and holds there through 2028. Global growth reaches 3.9% in 2027 (4Q/4Q) and the ECB holds at 3.5%.

Scenario 2, AI Productivity upside: productivity gains of about half a point a year let US growth exceed 3% by 2028 with inflation returning toward 2%. The Fed stays at 4.375% through 2028 because a higher r* makes it reluctant to cut while falling inflation prevents hikes.

Scenario 3, AI Investment downside: AI spending falls outright in 2027 because of power and construction bottlenecks. US growth slows to near 1%, unemployment exceeds 5%, and the Fed cuts to 1.875% at end-2027 and 1.375% at end-2028. Global growth falls below 3% and the ECB cuts to 0.75% by 2028.

Scenario 4, Rates and Oil downside: Middle East hostilities resume and oil rises to $125-150/bbl. The Fed hikes to 5.125% (5.375% in the narrative) and the US enters a mild recession in late 2027, with GDP of 1.6% in 2027 and 0.3% in 2028. Europe and the UK are also in recession, and easing is delayed to 2028 (Fed at 3.125% by end-2028).

MS does not model a falling-oil scenario because the baseline already assumes oil falling in line with market pricing, and the outcome would resemble a mix of the baseline and the productivity upside.

Fiscal: the US deficit stays near 6% of GDP (6.2% in 2026, 5.9% in 2027), with the fiscal impulse falling from about 40bp in 2026 to neutral in 2027. Treasury reliance on bills ahead of coupon increases shortens the maturity profile and speeds the pass-through of higher rates to deficits.

Debt sustainability has improved in the short run because of faster nominal growth: DM debt-to-GDP in 2030 is projected about 5pp lower than a year ago, but the medium-term outlook is worse as debt refinances at higher yields. France is the main euro area pressure point, with debt rising toward almost 160% of GDP by 2040 on current OAT yields. The UK is consolidating and gilts are trading more like a core market.

US policy: MS expects policy volatility to stay largely unchanged under divided government and sees scope for marginally higher tariffs after the midterms (USMCA review and Section 232 are the catalysts). The US-China base case is managed competition, with the Busan consensus components (178 Section 301 exclusions, BIS Affiliates Rule suspension, China's second-wave rare-earth controls) expiring in early January. AI data center restrictions are a state-level story.

Trade: the effective US tariff rate is lowered by the rising share of low-tariff AI hardware imports, but most consumer, capital and intermediate goods face tariffs above 10%. Evidence of reshoring is limited and the expected J-curve in capital-goods imports is not yet clearly visible. A USMCA resolution is the key catalyst for broader North American capex.

China: lowflation persists. Real GDP 4.6% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, CPI 0.7% in 2027, nominal growth slows to 4.8%, the PBoC holds policy rates at 1.25%, and the augmented deficit narrows to 10.5% of GDP in 2027. USD/CNY is forecast at 6.60 at end-2027 and 6.45 at end-2028.

Emerging markets: India's RBI is forecast to hike three more times to 6.25% by April 2027 (CPI averaging about 5% in 2027) before easing in 2028. Brazil holds at 13.75% through 2027 and cuts from 2028. Mexico makes a final cut to 6.0% in March 2027. Korea's BoK hikes to 3.5% by 1Q27, and Taiwan's CBC hikes to 2.25%.

Other notable calls: the Philippines' BSP hiked 50bp to 5.50% on November 9 with two more hikes expected. The RBA is at 4.85% after the November hike and is expected to cut in August and November 2027. The BoC hikes to 3.5% by end-2027 and Riksbank to 2.25% in February. Norges Bank holds at 4.5% until a December 2027 cut. Egypt's CBE hiked in October and resumes easing in 2Q27.
Saudi Arabia: real GDP contracts 1.6% in 2026 as oil export volumes fall, then rebounds 6.4% in 2027 as production normalizes in 2Q27. Egypt's base case assumes oil at $70-95/bbl in FY27 and FY28.

risk_factors: Energy shock turning nonlinear: energy, food and supply-chain pressures could push core inflation higher along with headline, and repeated supply shocks may shift inflation expectations and price setting.

AI capex shortfall or delay: an outright fall in 2027 spending would hit growth, asset prices and consumption together and prompt aggressive Fed easing. State-level data center restrictions in Texas and Ohio are a delay risk.
Rates and Oil downside: oil at $125-150/bbl with further central bank tightening, a mild US recession in late 2027 and recession in Europe and the UK.
Aggregate demand overheating: US unemployment at 3.5% and core inflation near 3% would force the Fed to 5.625%.
Diesel and refined product tightness into mid-2027, with historically wide refining spreads keeping fuel costs high even if crude falls. Europe is most exposed.
Fiscal and debt risks: France's non-consolidating deficit and wide OAT spreads, US bill-heavy Treasury financing, Brazil's fiscal trajectory, and the risk that nominal growth disappoints.
Overtightening and neutral-rate misestimation: central banks may be tightening toward neutral estimates inflated by supply shocks rather than demand.
Tariff re-escalation or an adverse USMCA outcome, and the possibility of marginally higher US tariffs after the midterms.
EM stress: tighter global financial conditions, with Egypt, the Philippines and Indonesia named as vulnerable (Egypt hiked 100bp in October amid FX pressure, rupiah weakness in Indonesia).
geopolitical: The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, though commodity strategists and market pricing point toward de-escalation. Resumed hostilities are the trigger for the Rates and Oil downside scenario with oil at $125-150/bbl.

US-China: base case is an extension of managed competition. The Busan consensus has three components expiring in early January: the 178 Section 301 exclusions, the BIS Affiliates Rule suspension and China's second-wave rare-earth controls. Watch the NDAA for export control legislation including the MATCH Act.

US midterm elections produced a divided Congress (Democratic House per the report). MS sees little practical policy impact on tariffs or geopolitics, and notes Congress can control defense funding on Iran.
The USMCA review and Section 232 sector tariffs are the key tariff catalysts for Mexico and Canada.
European elections: Spain, France (presidential April 2027, possible parliamentary elections in June) and Italy elections in 2027.
Attacks on oil and non-oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia have accelerated, per the Saudi Arabia section.

tension_points.bull_case: Faster AI productivity (about half a point a year) allows stronger US growth above 3% with inflation returning toward 2% and the Fed staying near 4.375%, without needing further tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: Stronger aggregate demand overheats the economy: unemployment falls to 3.5%, core inflation stays just above 3%, and the Fed must hike to 5.625% and hold through 2028.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that inflation fails to peak in 1Q27 and trend lower through 2027, or a sustained rise in US growth above 3% with unemployment toward 3.5%.

tension_points.bull_case: Baseline hyperscaler capex of $1.6tn in 2027 and $1.8tn in 2028 sustains US growth, with AI contributing over 1pp to US growth and software adoption taking over from infrastructure in 2028.
tension_points.bear_case: AI investment falls outright in 2027 because of power and construction bottlenecks, with US growth near 1%, unemployment above 5% and the Fed cutting to 1.375% by end-2028.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A shortfall in hyperscaler capex plans versus the $1.6tn 2027 forecast, or data center delays beyond the 5GW already shifted from 2028 to 2029.

tension_points.bull_case: Oil continues falling in line with market pricing and commodity strategists, headline inflation peaks in 1Q27 and central banks stop after one or two more hikes.
tension_points.bear_case: Renewed Middle East hostilities push oil to $125-150/bbl and refined products stay tight, forcing the Fed to 5.125%, a mild US recession in late 2027 and recessions in Europe and the UK.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Resumption of Gulf hostilities, or diesel and refined product prices staying elevated beyond mid-2027 even as crude falls.

theme_stances.key_argument: Persistent inflation from the energy shock keeps developed-market policy tighter, with the Fed, ECB and BoJ delivering a bit more tightening before easing in 2028.
theme_stances.evidence: monetary policy is anticipating the inflation pressure by tightening policy into the new year

theme_stances.key_argument: AI-driven capex and high-income consumption support US growth, though the GDP contribution peaks around 2027 and imports offset part of it.
theme_stances.evidence: AI capex is critical for both US growth and global growth through exports

theme_stances.key_argument: Wide refining spreads and tight diesel into mid-2027 mean falling crude may not lower fuel costs quickly, so central banks cannot look through the shock.
theme_stances.evidence: the price of crude oil on screens is no longer a sufficient statistic
